title: Motion without messages: four hair-trigger tips

trials.label: spot moving up and to the right, slow: the starting tip fires one tick too early to count, the far tip gives the answer
spot moving up and to the left, slow: the starting tip fires just as scoring begins and cancels the far tip
spot moving down and to the right, fast: only the far tip fires, on the last scored tick
spot moving left to right, slow: it passes between the arms and no cell fires

mechanism: The body is an X of 28 cells, but only the 4 cells at the tips of the X ever fire. The other 24 can never fire: their sensitivity to light is too weak to beat their built-in "stay quiet" setting, so they are just a skeleton that holds the tips out. The tips do send messages to their skeleton neighbours, but those messages only push already-silent cells further from firing, so switching messages off changes nothing. Each tip slowly charges up by itself in the dark, creeping toward its firing point without ever quite reaching it. The longer it has waited, the less light it takes to set it off. Starting from empty, a single flash would have to be 3 times the spot's full brightness (under the full spot held steady, it fires on its third tick). After 15 dark ticks, about 4% of the spot's brightness is enough. After firing it drops back to empty. The spot crosses the body in a straight line from one side to the other, and only the middle part of the trip is scored. A tip on the side the spot is heading toward waits in the dark and fires when the spot's light reaches it, late in the trip. For a slow spot that is a faint glow, about 4% of full brightness. A fast spot gives the tip less time to charge, so it fires on brighter light (about 40%), right on the last scored tick. One spike from that far tip earns almost full marks, because the tip itself lies in the direction the spot is going. The trick fails in two ways. First, a tip near where the spot starts also fires, right around the moment scoring begins. If the spot starts right on it, the spike comes one tick early and is not counted. If the spot starts a bit off and passes it a moment later, the spike lands inside the scored stretch and cancels the far tip's answer (about 1 trial in 4). Second, a spot moving roughly left to right passes between the two arms of the X, no tip gets enough light, and nothing fires (about 1 trial in 3). Each tip only answers "is light reaching me late in the trip?" from its own light, and that already points the way the spot is moving. That is why the motion task can be solved without communication, and why the project built the "jump" task to force cells to pass messages.
evidence: On 48 trials it had never seen (new directions, new speeds 0.75 and 1.5) it scores 0.41; on a bigger set of 960 such trials, 0.37. With messages switched off, the spike pattern is identical tick for tick on those trials and on 960 training trials. Only the 4 tip cells ever fire, and removing all 24 other cells at once leaves the score exactly the same (0.366 on the 960 new trials, 0.442 on training). How the 960 new trials end: 42% get spikes only on the side the spot is heading; 34% have no spike while scoring is on (mostly directions within 15 degrees of left-right); in 24% a starting-side tip fires inside the scored stretch, while it fires just before scoring in only 4%. Deleting every spike on the starting half would raise the score from 0.37 to 0.58 (training: 0.44 to 0.72). Scoring only the first half of the scored stretch gives -0.20 and only the second half 0.60 (48 trials). A single spike on the heading side scores a median of 0.97. The starting tip's timing follows where the spot starts (slow spots): when it fires too early to count, the light on it at the first tick was a median 61% of full; when it fires inside, only 29%, with its brightest light about 3 ticks in. Far-tip light at its scored spike: slow spots median 4% of full (10-90% range 2-9%), fast spots 39% (22-67%). In 65 of 472 fast trials the far tip fires one tick after scoring ends, which leaves the trial silent. Single-tip tests: 200 dark ticks give no spike; the one-tick flash needed is 3x full brightness from empty and 4% after 15 dark ticks; steady full light gives spikes at ticks 2 and 8. Knockouts (48 trials): removing any one tip costs 0.07-0.09, any other cell about 0; moving the two cell types around gives 0.18; making every cell the same type gives 0.01. A "start-of-trial clock" idea was tested and ruled out: charging every cell with 15 dark ticks before the trial raised the score (0.41 to 0.56; 0.37 to 0.55 on 960 trials) instead of breaking it. The gain comes mainly from fully charged tips firing on even the faintest glow, so silent trials almost vanish (325 to 16 of 960).
